The lexicographers said: it is said of a man who persists in his journey: "He labored (ʿamila yaʿmalu ʿamalan)," and it is said of a cloud when its lightning persists: "It has labored (qad ʿamila yaʿmalu ʿamalan)."

It has been said that this work is dragging chains and shackles and wading through the Fire. *Nāṣibah* means weary (*taʿibah*). It is said *nasiba* (with a kasra) *yansabu nasaban*, meaning he became weary. The meaning is that in the Hereafter they will be weary because of what they encounter of Allah's punishment.

It has also been said that His words ﴿working, toiling﴾ refer to this world, since there is no work in the Hereafter. That is, they labour in this world in disbelief and sin, and they toil in that.

It has also been said that they labour in this world and toil in the Hereafter. The first view is preferable.

Qatadah said: ﴿Working, toiling﴾ means that they were arrogant in this world toward obedience to Allah, so Allah made them labour and toil in the Fire by dragging heavy chains, carrying shackles, and standing barefoot and naked in the open plains ﴿on a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Maʿārij: 4]. Al-Ḥasan and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: they did not labour for Allah in this world and did not toil, so Allah made them labour and toil in Jahannam.

Al-Kalbi said: they will be dragged on their faces in the Fire.

He also said: they will be burdened with climbing a mountain of iron in Jahannam, and they will toil there with the utmost toil, handling chains and shackles and wading through the Fire, as camels wade through mud.

The majority of readers (*qurrāʾ*, reciters; *qirāʾāt*, recitations, meaning the authorised variant readings of the Qur'an) read ﴿working, toiling﴾ with *rafʿ* (nominative) in both words, on the basis that they are two further predicates of the subject, or on the basis of an implied subject, and they are predicates of it. Ibn Muḥaysin, ʿĪsā, Ḥumayd, and Ibn Kathīr in one narration from him read both with *naṣb* (accusative), as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) or as a term of blame (*dhamm*).

His words ﴿they will enter a blazing Fire﴾ are another predicate of the subject. That is, they will enter a fire extremely intense in heat. It is said *ḥamiya al-nahār* and *ḥamiya al-tannūr*, meaning their heat intensified.

Al-Kisāʾi said: it is said *ishtadda ḥamy al-nahār* and *ḥamwuhu*, with the same meaning.

The majority read *taṣlā* with a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ*, in the active voice. Abu ʿAmr, Yaʿqub, and Abu Bakr read both *tuṣlā* and *tusqā* with a *ḍammah*, in the passive voice.

Abu Rajāʾ read it with a *ḍammah* on the *tāʾ*, a *fatḥah* on the *ṣād*, and a *shaddah* on the *lām*. The pronoun refers to the faces (*wujūh*) in all these recitations, and the intended meaning is their owners, as mentioned earlier. The same applies to the pronoun.

﴿They will be given drink from a boiling spring﴾. What is meant by the boiling spring (*ʿayn āniyah*) is one extremely intense in heat. *Ānī* is that which has reached its utmost heat, from *al-īnāʾ*, meaning delay. It is said *ānāhu yuʾnīhi īnāʾan*, meaning he delayed and detained him, as in His words: ﴿They will go round between it and a scalding, boiling water﴾ [al-Raḥmān: 44]. Al-Wāḥidi said: the commentators said that if a single drop of it fell on the mountains of this world, they would melt.

When He, glorified is He, mentioned their drink, He followed it with mention of their food, saying: ﴿They will have no food except from ḍarīʿ﴾. *Ḍarīʿ* is a kind of thorny plant called *shibriq* in the language of Quraysh when it is fresh; when it dries out, it becomes *ḍarīʿ*.

Mujāhid, Qatadah, and other commentators said this.

It has been said that it is a deadly poison, and that when it dries out no animal approaches it or grazes on it. It has also been said that it is something the sea casts up, called *ḍarīʿ*, which is food for livestock and not for people. When camels graze on it they do not become sated and perish from emaciation.

Al-Khalīl said: *ḍarīʿ* is a green plant with a foul smell that the sea casts up.

The majority of the lexicographers and commentators said the first view. From it is the verse of Abū Dhuʾayb:

*He grazed on the lush shibriq until it withered and became ḍarīʿ, and the tahāyis [a kind of bramble] departed from it.*

And al-Hudhalī, describing camels and their poor pasture, said:

*A pen of withered ḍarīʿ, and all of them are thin, with scraped hides, bloodied in both forelegs, and worn.*

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: *ḍarīʿ* means stones. It has also been said that it is a tree in the Fire of Jahannam.

Al-Ḥasan said: it is part of the punishment that Allah has kept hidden.

Ibn Kaysān said: it is a food at which they humble themselves, abase themselves, and beseech Allah to be delivered from it. It is named so because whoever eats it implores Allah to spare him, because of its repulsiveness and harshness.

Al-Naḥḥās said: it may be derived from *al-ḍāriʿ*, meaning the humble one. That is, from drinking it one is afflicted with humility and abasement.

Al-Ḥasan also said: it is *al-zaqqūm*. It has also been said that it is a valley in Jahannam. This has already been mentioned in Sūrat al-Ḥāqqah: ﴿So today he has no friend here, nor any food except from ghislīn﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 35–36]. *Ghislīn* is other than *ḍarīʿ*, as mentioned previously. The two verses were reconciled by saying that the Fire has levels (*darakāt*): some of its people have *ḍarīʿ* as their food, and others have *ghislīn*.

Then He, glorified is He, described *ḍarīʿ*, saying: ﴿It neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger﴾. That is, *ḍarīʿ* does not fatten the one who eats it, nor does it relieve the hunger he has.

The commentators said: when this verse was revealed, the polytheists said: our camels grow fat on *ḍarīʿ*. Then ﴿It neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger﴾ was revealed. They lied in what they said, for camels do not eat *ḍarīʿ* and do not go near it.

It has also been said that its nature was confused for them, so they assumed it was like other beneficial plants.

Then He, glorified is He, began to explain the state of the people of Paradise after finishing with the state of the people of the Fire, saying: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant﴾. That is, possessing blessing and brightness. These are the faces of the believers, whose faces became radiant because of what they witnessed of the outcome of their affair and of what Allah has prepared for them of good that exceeds description. A similar verse is His words: ﴿You will recognise in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾ [al-Muṭaffifīn: 24].

Then He said: ﴿Pleased with their striving﴾. That is, pleased with the deed they performed in this world, because they have been given reward that satisfied them and gladdened their eyes. Here "faces" refers to their owners, as mentioned earlier.

﴿In an elevated Garden﴾. That is, elevated in place, raised above other places; or elevated in rank, because in it is what souls desire and eyes delight in.

﴿In which they will hear no idle talk﴾. Al-Jumhūr read *lā tasmaʿu* with a *fatḥah* on the second-person *tāʾ* and *naṣb* on *lāghiyah*, meaning: you, O addressee, will not hear, or those faces will not hear.

Ibn Kathīr and Abu ʿAmr read it with a *ḍammah* on the *yāʾ*, in the passive voice, and *rafʿ* on *lāghiyah*.

Nāfiʿ read it with a *ḍammah* on the *tāʾ*, in the passive voice, and *rafʿ* on *lāghiyah*.

Al-Faḍl and al-Jaḥdarī read it with a *fatḥah* on the *yāʾ*, in the active voice, and *naṣb* on *lāghiyah*.

*Laghw* is futile, fallen speech. Al-Farrāʾ and al-Akhfash said: that is, they will not hear in it a word of idle talk.

It has been said that what is meant is lies, falsehood, and disbelief. Qatadah said this. Mujāhid said: that is, insult.

Al-Farrāʾ said: they will not hear in it one swearing an oath falsely.

Al-Kalbi said: they will not hear in Paradise anyone swearing an oath, whether a truthful or a sinful one.

Al-Farrāʾ also said: they will not hear in the speech of the people of Paradise any word that is idle, because they speak only with wisdom and praise of Allah, exalted is He, for what He has provided them of everlasting bliss. This is the most preferred of the views, because an indefinite noun in a negative context is a form of generality, and there is no basis for restricting this to a particular kind of idle talk except by a specifier that is suitable for restriction. *Lāghiyah* is either an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning *kalimah lāghiyah* (an idle word) or *nafs lāghiyah* (an idle soul), or a verbal noun, meaning: they will not hear in it *laghwan* (idle talk).

﴿In it is a flowing spring﴾. It has already been mentioned in Sūrat al-Insān that in it are springs, and *ʿayn* here carries the meaning of *ʿuyūn* (springs), as in His words: ﴿Every soul will know﴾ [al-Takwīr: 14]. *Jāriyah* (flowing) means that its waters flow and gush forth with kinds of delicious drinks.

Al-Kalbi said: I do not know whether it is water or something else.

﴿In it are raised couches﴾. That is, lofty, high in height; or lofty in rank.

﴿And cups placed [ready]﴾. It has already been mentioned that *akwāb* is the plural of *kūb*, which is a cup without a handle. *Mawḍūʿah* (placed) means they are placed before them, from which they drink.

﴿And cushions arranged in rows﴾. *Namāriq* are cushions.

Al-Wāḥidi said: by the agreement of all, its singular is *numruqah* with a *ḍammah* on the *nūn*. Al-Farrāʾ added, from the Arabs by hearing, *nimriqah* with a *kasrah*.

Al-Kalbi said: cushions arranged, some next to others. From this is the poet's saying:

*Indeed we pass the cup among our drinking companions, and between Abū Qābūs upon the cushions.*

And another said:

*Elders and youths, beautiful of face, upon couches arranged in rows, and cushions.*

In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* it is said: *al-numruq* and *al-nimriqah* is a small cushion, and likewise *al-nimriqah* with a *kasrah* is a dialect reported by Yaʿqūb.

﴿And carpets spread out﴾. This means rugs. Its singular is *zurbī* and *zurbiyyah*.

Abū ʿUbaydah and al-Farrāʾ said: *al-zarābī* are the cloths with a fine nap, its singular being *zarbiyyah*. *Mabthūthah* means spread out; Qatadah said this.

Ikrimah said: some of them upon others.

Al-Wāḥidi said: it could also mean that they are scattered throughout the gatherings. Al-Qutaybi said this too.

Al-Farrāʾ said: the meaning of *mabthūthah* is abundant. The apparent meaning of *al-baththu* is dispersal with abundance, as in His words: ﴿And He spread throughout them every kind of creature﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164].

﴿Will they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach, and the *fāʾ* is for coordination with an implied element, as in its parallels that have occurred more than once. The sentence is directed toward establishing the matter of resurrection and providing evidence for it, and so is what follows. *Kayfa* is in the accusative, governed by what follows it, and the clause is in the genitive position, as a substitute of inclusion (*badal ishtimāl*) for "camels." The meaning: do they deny the matter of resurrection and consider its occurrence far-fetched? Will they not look at the camels, which are the majority of their livestock and the greatest of the creatures they see, ﴿how they were created﴾ in the wondrous creation they have, with the greatness of their bodies, their great strength, and their wondrous attributes?

Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said: He specified camels because they are among the quadrupeds that kneel down so that the loads can be put on them, whereas other quadrupeds are not loaded unless they are standing. Al-Zajjāj said: He alerted them to a great creature of His creation, which He has made docile for the small child: he leads it, makes it kneel, makes it rise, and carries heavy loads on it while it is kneeling, so it rises with the weight of its load. No other load-bearing animal does this. Thus He showed them a great part of His creation, so that by this it would point to His oneness.

Al-Ḥasan was asked about this verse, and it was said to him that the elephant is more wondrous. He said: as for the elephant, the Arabs are far removed from it in time; moreover, it is a pig that is not ridden on its back, its meat is not eaten, and its milk is not milked. Camels are among the most valuable and precious property of the Arabs: they eat date pits and fodder, they yield milk, and a boy takes hold of their halter and leads them wherever he wishes, despite their great size in themselves.

Al-Mubarrad said: *al-ibil* here means great pieces of cloud. This differs from what the commentators and lexicographers have mentioned.

It is related from al-Aṣmaʿī that he said: whoever reads *khuliqat* with the light form means the camel, and whoever reads it with the doubled form means the clouds.

﴿And at the sky, how it was raised﴾. That is, raised above the earth without pillars, in a manner that understanding cannot grasp and the intellect cannot comprehend. It has been said: it was raised so that nothing can reach it.

﴿And at the mountains, how they were set firm﴾ on the earth, fixed and firmly rooted, not swaying, not leaning, and not moving.

﴿And at the earth, how it was spread out﴾. That is, it was spread flat. *Saṭḥ* is the spreading of a thing; it is said of the roof of a house when it is level: *saṭḥ*.

Al-Jumhūr read *suṭiḥat* in the passive voice, lightened. Al-Ḥasan read it with the doubled form.

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ, and Abū al-ʿĀliyah read: *khalaqtu, rafaʿtu, naṣabtu, saṭaḥtu*, in the active voice, with a *ḍammah* on the *tāʾ* in all of them.

Then He, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to remind, saying: ﴿So remind﴾. The *fāʾ* indicates the sequence of what follows relative to what precedes: that is, admonish them, O Muḥammad, and warn them.

Then He gave the reason for the command to remind, saying: ﴿You are only a reminder﴾. That is, nothing is incumbent upon you except that.

﴿You are not over them a controller﴾. *Al-muṣayṭir* and *al-musayṭir*, with *sīn* and *ṣād*, means one empowered over a thing to oversee it and attend to its affairs, as stated in *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*. That is: you are not over them a controller, to the point of compelling them to faith. This verse has been abrogated by the verse of the sword.

Al-Jumhūr read *bi-muṣayṭir* with a *ṣād*. Hishām and Qunbul in one narration read it with a *sīn*.

Khalaf read it with the *ṣād* pronounced as a *zāy* (*ishmām*).

Hārūn al-Aʿwar read it with a *fatḥah* on the *ṭāʾ* as a passive participle.

﴿Except for whoever turns away and disbelieves﴾. This is an exceptive clause of disconnection (*istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ*). That is: but whoever turns away from admonition and reminder.

﴿So Allah will punish him with the greatest punishment﴾, which is the everlasting punishment of Hell. It has also been said that this is a continuous exception (istithna' muttasil) from His words ﴿so remind﴾, meaning: remind everyone except the one whose hope of his faith you have lost and who turns away, and so deserves the greatest punishment. The first view is preferable.

He said "the greatest" because they were punished in this world by hunger, drought, killing and captivity.

Ibn Mas'ud recited ﴿Indeed, it is He who will punish him﴾ (fa-innahu yu'adhdhibuhu Allah). Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah recited "Alā man tawallā" (Surely whoever turns away), taking "alā" as the particle of alerting and opening (al-tanbih wa al-istiftah).

﴿Indeed, to Us is their return﴾, i.e., their coming back after death. It is said: āba yaūbu, meaning he returned. From this is the saying of 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras:

*Every absent one returns, but the absence of death does not return.*

The majority (al-Jumhur) read *iyābahum* with a light pronunciation (takhfif). Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read it with a doubled letter (tashdid).

Abu Hatim said: the doubling is not permissible; if it were, its equivalent would be permissible in *al-siyām* and *al-qiyām*. It has also been said that both are two dialects with the same meaning.

al-Wahidi said: as for *iyābahum* with a doubled yā', it is anomalous (shādh), and no one permitted it except al-Zajjaj.

﴿Then indeed upon Us is their reckoning﴾, meaning their recompense after their return to Allah through resurrection. *Thumma* (then) here indicates a delay in rank, because the station of reckoning is far greater in severity than the station of return.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "al-Ghashiyah" is among the names of the Resurrection.

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him regarding ﴿Has there come to you the news of the Overwhelming?﴾, that it is the Hour. ﴿Faces that Day will be humbled, labouring and weary﴾: he said, they will labour and toil in the Fire. ﴿Given to drink from a boiling spring﴾: he said, it is the one whose heat has reached its extreme. ﴿They will have no food except from *dari'*﴾: he said, it is *al-shibriq*.

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him: ﴿Faces that Day will be humbled, labouring and weary﴾, he said: this means the Jews and Christians, who humble themselves, but their deeds will not benefit them. ﴿Given to drink from a boiling spring﴾: he said, its boiling has reached its end.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him regarding His words ﴿They will burn in a fierce fire﴾: he said, hot. ﴿Given to drink from a boiling spring﴾: he said, its heat has reached its limit. ﴿They will have no food except from *dari'*﴾: he means, from a tree of fire.

'Abd ibn Humayd also narrated from him: ﴿except from *dari'*﴾, he said: dried *shibriq*.

Ibn Jarir also narrated from him: ﴿Therein they will hear no idle talk﴾, meaning they will hear neither harm nor falsehood. Regarding His words ﴿Therein are raised couches﴾, he said: some above others. ﴿And cushions set out﴾, he said: gatherings.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him: ﴿And cushions set out﴾, he said: the armrests (al-marafiq).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him regarding ﴿You are not over them a controller﴾: he said, a tyrant. ﴿Except one who turns away and disbelieves﴾: he said, his reckoning is upon Allah.

Abu Dawud, in his book *al-Nasikh*, narrated from him regarding ﴿You are not over them a controller﴾ that it was then abrogated (nasakha) by His words: ﴿So kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5].

Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him regarding ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return﴾: he said, their place of return.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 87, verses 1–19 (part 1 of 4):

It is Meccan according to the majority of scholars.

Al-Dahhak said: it is Medinan.

Ibn al-Duraysi, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "The surah ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn al-Zubayr and ʿAʾishah something similar.

Al-Bukhari and others transmitted from al-Baraʾ ibn ʿAzib that he said: "The first of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ to come to us was Musʿab ibn ʿUmayr and Ibn Umm Maktum. They began teaching us the Qur'an. Then ʿAmmar, Bilal and Saʿd came. Then ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab came with twenty men. Then the Prophet ﷺ came. I have never seen the people of Medina rejoice at anything as they rejoiced at him, until I saw the young women and children saying, 'This is the Messenger of God ﷺ, who has come.' He had not arrived until I had recited ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ and a surah like it."

Ahmad, al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from ʿAli that he said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ loved this surah: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾."

Ahmad, Muslim and the authors of the Sunan transmitted from al-Nuʿman ibn Bashir that "the Messenger of God ﷺ used to recite in the two ʿIds and on Friday ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ and ﴿Has there come to you the report of the Overwhelming?﴾. If the ʿId fell on a Friday, he recited both of them together." In another wording: "Sometimes both came together on one day, and he recited them both." There are other hadiths on this topic.

Muslim and others transmitted from Jabir ibn Samurah that "the Prophet ﷺ used to recite ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ in the noon prayer."

Abu Dawud, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Majah, al-Daraqutni, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that he said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ used to pray the witr with ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾, ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾, and ﴿Say: He is God, One﴾."

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim (who authenticated it) and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from ʿAʾishah that she said: "The Prophet ﷺ used to recite in the witr, in the first rakʿah, ﴿Glorify﴾, in the second ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾, and in the third ﴿Say: He is God, One﴾ and the two protective surahs." In the two Sahihs it is reported that the Messenger of God ﷺ said to Muʿadh: "Why did you not pray with ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾, ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾, and ﴿By the night when it covers﴾?" [i.e., Surah al-Layl].

[p-1611]
In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

His words: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾, meaning: declare Him free of everything that is not fitting for Him.

Al-Suddi said: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ means: magnify Him. It has been said that the word "name" (ism) here is superfluous (muqhamah), for the purpose of glorification, as in the verse of Labid:

*Until the year is complete, then "the name of peace be upon you both,"*
*and whoever weeps for a full year has excused himself.*

The meaning is: glorify your Lord, the Most High.

Ibn Jarir said: the meaning is, "Declare the name of your Lord free of being named by anyone other than Him." Thus, on this view, it is not superfluous.

It has also been said that the meaning is: declare the naming of your Lord and your mention of Him free of [being mentioned] except with humility and reverence, and with respect for His remembrance.

Al-Hasan said: the meaning of ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ is: pray to Him.

It has been said the meaning is: pray with the names of God, not as the polytheists pray, with whistling and clapping.

It has also been said the meaning is: raise your voice in the remembrance of your Lord. From this is the verse of Jarir:

*May God disfigure the faces of Taghlib, whenever*
*the pilgrims glorify and magnify with great magnification.*

"The Most High" (al-aʿla) is an attribute of the Lord, and it has been said it is an attribute of "name." The first view is preferable.

His words: ﴿Who created and proportioned﴾ are another attribute of the Lord.

Al-Zajjaj said: He created man upright, and the meaning of "proportioned" (sawwa) is that He made his stature balanced.

Al-Dahhak said: He created him and made his creation proportionate. It has been said He created bodies and made the faculties proportionate. It has been said He created man and prepared him for moral responsibility (taklif).

﴿And who determined and guided﴾ is another attribute of the Lord, or it is coordinated (maʿtuf) with the relative clause before it.

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, al-Kisaʾi and al-Sulami read "qadara" (determined) with light stress (mukhaffafan), while the rest read it with the doubled letter (al-tashdid). Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: He determined the creation of the male and female of the animals, and He guided the male to the female, [showing him] how to approach her.

Mujahid said: He guided man to the path of good and evil, and to happiness and misery.

It is also reported from him that he said regarding the meaning of the verse: He determined happiness and misery, and He guided to right guidance and to error, and He guided the livestock to their pasturage.

It has been said He determined their provisions and sustenance, and guided them to their livelihoods if they were human, and to their pasture if they were wild.

ʿAtaʾ said: For every creature was provided what sustains it, and He guided it to it.

It has been said He created the benefits in things, and guided man to the method of extracting them from them.

Al-Suddi said: He determined the duration of the fetus in the womb as nine months, or less or more, then He guided it to come out of the womb.

Al-Farraʾ said: That is, He determined and guided, and He led astray, and one of the two was sufficient. There are views on the interpretation of the verse other than those we have mentioned.

The preferable view is not to specify one individual or several of what the words "determined" and "guided" might apply to, unless there is evidence indicating it. In the absence of evidence, the verse is taken to refer to whatever the meaning of the two verbs covers, either by substitution (ʿala al-badal) or by comprehensiveness (ʿala al-shumul). The meaning is: He determined the kinds of things, their species, their attributes, their actions, their words, and their terms, and He guided each one of them to what proceeds from it and what befits it, facilitated for it what it was created for, and inspired it toward the affairs of its religion and its worldly life.

﴿And who brought forth the pasture﴾ is another attribute of the Lord: that is, He caused the herbage and the green vegetation that livestock graze to grow.

﴿Then made it dry stubble, dark⟩ — that is, after it had been green, He made it stubble, meaning dried, brittle debris like the scum that lies atop a flood; ﴿dark﴾ means black after its greenness. This is because when herbage dries it turns black.

Qatadah said: "Ghuthaʾ" is dry matter. It is said of the green herb and grass when it is crushed and dried: "ghuthaʾ" and "hashim" (dry brittle stalks).

Imru al-Qays said:

*As if the peaks of the head of al-Mujaymir at morning*
*were, from the flood and the scum, a spindle whorl.*

The accusative of "ghuthaʾ" is either as the second object, or as a circumstantial accusative (hal). "Ahwa" is an attribute of it.

Al-Kisaʾi said: It is a circumstantial accusative from "the pasture": that is, He brought it forth dark from the intensity of greenness and moisture, then made it stubble after that. "Ahwa" is derived from "al-hawwa," which is blackness tending toward green.

Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: "al-hawwah" is the darkness of the lip, and from this is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

*A honey-lipped one, on whose lips is the darkness of the lips' dark sweetness,*
*and on her gums and her fangs is a sweet coolness.*

﴿We shall make you recite, so you will not forget﴾: that is, We shall make you a reciter by inspiring you to recite, so you will not forget what you recite. The sentence is resumed (mustaʾnafah), explaining his special guidance ﷺ after the explanation of general guidance; it is his guidance ﷺ for memorizing the Qur'an.

Mujahid and al-Kalbi said: "When Gabriel came to the Prophet ﷺ with revelation, Gabriel would not finish the last part of the verse before the Prophet ﷺ began speaking the first part of it, for fear that he would forget it. So the verse ﴿We shall make you recite, so you will not forget﴾ was revealed."

His words: ﴿except what God wills﴾ are an exception of the "emptied" type (istithnaʾ mufarragh, i.e., an exception where the excluded element is left unspecified) from the most general of the objects: that is, you will not forget any of the things you recite, except what God wills that you forget.

Al-Farraʾ said: He, glorified be He, did not will that Muhammad ﷺ forget anything, like His saying: ﴿Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾ [Hud: 107]. It has also been said: except what God wills that you forget and then remember afterwards. Thus he has forgotten, but he remembers, and he does not forget anything with complete forgetfulness.

It has been said the meaning is abrogation (naskh): that is, except what God wills to abrogate its recitation.

It has been said the meaning of "so you will not forget" is: so do not abandon acting upon it, except what God wills that you abandon because of its abrogation and the lifting of its ruling.

It has been said the meaning is: except what God wills to delay its sending down.

It has been said that "lā" in His saying ﴿so you will not forget﴾ is a prohibition (nahy). The alif is added for the sake of the rhyme (fasila), as in His saying: ﴿So they led us astray from the way﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67]. That is, do not neglect its recitation, and remember it.

﴿Indeed He knows the open and what is hidden﴾: the sentence is a justification (taʿlil) for what precedes it, that is: He knows what appears and what is concealed, and what is proclaimed and what is kept secret. Its apparent meaning is generality, so it includes what has been said: the "open" is what the Messenger of God ﷺ memorized of the Qur'an, and "what is hidden" is what was abrogated from his breast. It also includes what has been said: the "open" is the public declaration of charity, and "what is hidden" is concealing it. It also includes what has been said: the "open" is his ﷺ reciting the Qur'an aloud along with Gabriel's recitation, for fear that it might slip from him, and "what is hidden" is what is in his soul that calls him to recite aloud.

﴿And We shall ease you toward ease﴾ is coordinated with ﴿We shall make you recite﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (iʿtiraḍ).

Muqatil said: that is, We shall make the work of Paradise easy for you. It has been said: We shall grant you success in the way that is easiest and simplest. It has been said: [We shall grant you success for] the easy Law, which is the simple, straight religion (al-hanifiyyah al-samhah). It has been said: We shall make the revelation easy for you, until you memorize it and act upon it. The preferable view is to take the verse in its generality: that is, We shall grant you success in the easiest path, in religion and in worldly life, in every matter of the two that comes before you.

﴿So remind, if the reminder benefits﴾: that is, admonish people, O Muhammad, with what We have revealed to you, direct them to the paths of good, and guide them to the laws of the religion.

Al-Hasan said: It is a reminder for the believer and a proof against the disbeliever.

Al-Wahidi said: [it means] whether it benefits or does not benefit, and he did not mention the second case, like His saying: ﴿Garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], and so on.

Al-Jurjani said: Reminding is obligatory even if it does not benefit, so the meaning is: whether the reminder benefits or does not benefit.

It has been said that this is specific to a particular group of people. It has been said: "in" (in) here means "what" (ma): that is, remind of what the reminder benefits, because the reminder is beneficial in every case. It has been said that it means "indeed" (qad), and it has been said that it means "when" (idh).

What al-Wahidi and al-Jurjani said is preferable, and al-Farraʾ and al-Nahhas preceded them in saying it.

Al-Razi said: His saying ﴿if the reminder benefits﴾ draws attention to the more noble of the two states, namely the existence of the benefit for which the reminder was prescribed. A conditional with "in" on something does not require that its opposite be the case when that thing is absent. Several verses show this: among them this verse; among them His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and give thanks to God, if you are indeed those who worship Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 172]; among them His saying: ﴿there is no blame upon you if you shorten the prayer, if you fear﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 101], since shortening the prayer is permitted both in fear and in its absence; and among them His saying: ﴿there is no blame upon them both if they return to one another, if they think that they can keep within the limits of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230], since returning is permitted without this thought. So this condition has benefits: among them what has preceded, and among them the urging to benefit from the reminder, as a man says to one he is guiding: "I have explained it to you clearly, if you have understanding." It is an admonition to the Prophet ﷺ that they will not benefit from the reminder. Or this may be about the repetition of the call, whereas the first call is general. End of quotation.

Then He, glorified be He, made clear the difference between the one whom the reminder benefits and the one whom it does not benefit, and He said: ﴿He who fears will be reminded﴾, that is, the one who fears God will be admonished by your admonition, and so he will increase in fear and in righteousness through the reminder.

﴿But the most wretched will avoid it﴾: that is, the most wretched of the disbelievers will shun the reminder and keep far from it, because of his persistence in disbelief in God and his immersion in His disobedience.

Then He described the most wretched, saying: ﴿who will burn in the greatest Fire﴾: that is, the great, terrible one, because it is more intense in heat than other fires.

Al-Hasan said: "The greatest Fire" is the Fire of Hell. "The lesser fire" is the fire of this world.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is the lowest of the layers of the Fire.

﴿Then he will neither die therein nor live﴾: that is, he will not die therein so that he may find rest from the punishment he is in, nor will he live a life from which he benefits. From this is the verse of the poet:

*Ah, for a soul that does not die, so that its hardship ends,*
*nor lives a life that has any sweetness.*

"Then" (thumma) here indicates delay in degrees of severity, because wavering between death and life is more dreadful than burning in the greatest Fire.

﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies himself﴾: that is, whoever purifies himself from polytheism, believes in God, affirms His oneness, and acts according to His laws.

ʿAtaʾ and al-Rabiʿ said: whoever's deed is pure and growing.

Qatadah said: he purifies himself by a righteous deed.

Qatadah, ʿAtaʾ and Abu al-ʿAliyah said: it was revealed concerning the charity of the fast-breaking (zakat al-fitr).

Ikrimah said: A man would say, "I present my zakat before my prayer."

The root meaning of "zakah" in the language is growth.

It has been said the verse means the zakat of all wealth.

It has been said the verse means the zakat of deeds, not the zakat of wealth, because the more common usage for wealth is "zakka" (he purified it), not "tazakka" (he purified himself).

He invoked the name of his Lord and prayed. It has been said that the meaning is: he remembered his Lord with fear, so he worshipped Him and prayed to Him. It has also been said: he invoked the name of his Lord with his tongue and prayed, meaning he established the five daily prayers.

It has also been said: he remembered his standing before his Lord and his return to Him, so he worshipped Him, and this is similar to the first opinion.

It has also been said: he invoked the name of his Lord through the takbir (saying "Allahu Akbar") at the beginning of the prayer, since the prayer is not validly begun except with His remembrance, and that is his saying "Allahu Akbar." It has also been said: he invoked the name of his Lord on the way to the prayer-place and then prayed. It has also been said that it means he performs a voluntary prayer after giving charity (zakat).

It has also been said that the prayer meant here is the Eid prayer, just as the purification (tazakki) in the first verse means the zakat al-fitr (charity at the end of Ramadan). But after this view, there is no doubt of its weakness, because the surah is Meccan, and zakat al-fitr and the Eid prayer were only made obligatory in Medina.

﴿But you prefer the worldly life﴾: this is an idrab (a turning away from a previous statement, marked by "bal," "rather"), referring to an unstated speech that the context implies. The meaning is: you do not do this, but rather you prefer the fleeting pleasures of the world.

The majority of readers (qurra') read tu'thirūna (تُؤْثِرُونَ) with a ta (فوقية, the letter above the line), in the second-person address. Its support is the reading of Ubayy: "bal antum tu'thirūna" (بَلْ أنْتُمْ تُؤْثِرُونَ). Abu 'Amr read it with a ya (تحتية, the letter below the line), in the third-person (ghaybah).

It has been said that the verse refers to the disbelievers, and that preferring the worldly life means being satisfied with it, feeling at ease with it, and turning away from the Hereafter altogether. It has also been said that it refers to all people, believers and disbelievers alike, and that preferring it means something more general, which most people cannot avoid: the worldly side taking precedence over the Hereafter, turning toward gaining its benefits, and being preoccupied with them to a degree greater than their preoccupation with acts of obedience.

﴿And the Hereafter is better and more lasting﴾: this is in the accusative position (fi mahall nasb) as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of tu'thirūna. The meaning is: while the true state is that the abode of the Hereafter, which is Paradise, is better and more enduring than the world.

Mālik ibn Dīnār said: "If the world were gold that perishes, and the Hereafter were clay that lasts, it would be obligatory to prefer the clay that lasts over the gold that perishes. How much more so when the Hereafter is gold that lasts and the world is clay that perishes?"

The reference in His saying ﴿Indeed, this﴾ is to what was mentioned before, namely the success of the one who purifies himself and what follows it. It has also been said that it refers to the entire surah. The meaning of ﴿is in the former scriptures﴾ is that it is established in them.

His saying ﴿the scriptures of Abraham and Moses﴾ is a badal (a substitute or apposition, replacing) for ﴿the former scriptures﴾.

Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: by His saying "Indeed, this" he means that the Hereafter is better and more lasting. And they said: the books of God, mighty and majestic, agreed that the Hereafter is better and more lasting than the world.

Al-Hasan said: the books of God, whose praise is exalted, agreed that ﴿indeed, this is in the former scriptures﴾, and that is His saying ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself﴾ up to the end of the surah.

The majority read ﴿lafī al-suḥuf al-ūlā ṣuḥufi Ibrāhīm﴾ with a ḍamma on the ḥā' (ḥarakat) in both places. Al-A'mash, Harun, and Abu 'Amr in one narration from him read them with a sukūn (no vowel) on the ḥā' in both places. The majority read Ibrāhīm with an alif after the rā' and a yā' after the hā'. Abu Raja' read it without those two letters and with a fatḥa on the hā'. Abu Musa and Ibn al-Zubayr read it "Ibrāhām" with two alifs.

Aḥmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Uqba ibn 'Āmir al-Juhanī, who said: «When [the verse] ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 52] was revealed, the Messenger of God ﷺ said to us: "Make it in your bowing (rukū')." When [the verse] "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High" [i.e., the surah al-A'lā] was revealed, he said: "Make it in your prostration (sujūd)."» There is no fault in its chain.

Aḥmad, Abu Dawud, al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that «when the Messenger of God ﷺ recited ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ he would say: "Subḥāna Rabbiya al-A'lā (Glory be to my Lord, the Most High)."»

Abu Dawud said: Waki' contradicted this, for Shu'ba narrated it from Abu Ishaq, from Sa'id, from Ibn 'Abbas, as a statement of Ibn 'Abbas (mawqūf) and not as a statement of the Prophet ﷺ.

'Abd al-Razzāq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Jarir also narrated it as a mawqūf statement from Ibn 'Abbas, that when he recited "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High" he would say: "Subḥāna Rabbiya al-A'lā." In a wording from 'Abd ibn Humayd from him: "When you recite 'Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High,' then say: 'Subḥāna Rabbiya al-A'lā.'"

Al-Firyābī, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Anbārī in al-Maṣāḥif narrated from 'Alī ibn Abi Ṭālib that he recited ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ and said: "Subḥāna Rabbiya al-A'lā," while he was in prayer. He was asked: "Do you add to the Qur'an?" He said: "No, but He commanded us with something, so I said it."

Al-Firyābī, Sa'īd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'arī that he recited "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High" on Friday and said: "Subḥāna Rabbiya al-A'lā."

Sa'īd ibn Manṣūr, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, narrated from Sa'īd ibn Jubayr who said: "I heard Ibn 'Umar reciting '﻿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High,' and he said: 'Subḥāna Rabbiya al-A'lā.'" And it is thus in the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from 'Abd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr that he recited ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ and said: "Subḥāna Rabbiya al-A'lā," while he was in prayer.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿then made it debris (ghuthā')﴾, that he said: "Dry crumbled stalks (hashīman)." And [regarding] "dark green" (aḥwā) he said: "Changed (mutaghayyiran)."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him, who said: «The Prophet ﷺ used to review the Qur'an out of fear that he would forget it, so it was said to him: "We have spared you that," and [the verse] was revealed: ﴿We will make you recite, and you will not forget﴾.»

Al-Ḥākim narrated similar from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqāṣ.

Ibn Abi Ḥātim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿except what God wills﴾: "Except what I will, then I will make you forget."

Ibn Abi Ḥātim also narrated from him ﴿And We will ease you toward ease﴾ and said: "Toward good."

Ibn Abi Ḥātim narrated from Ibn Mas'ūd ﴿And We will ease you toward ease﴾ and said: "Paradise."

Al-Bazzār and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Jābir ibn 'Abd Allāh «from the Prophet ﷺ regarding His saying ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself﴾, that he said: "Whoever testifies that there is no god but God, and abandons rivals (andād), and testifies that I am the Messenger of God." ﴿And remembers the name of his Lord and prays﴾: "These are the five prayers, and maintaining them and caring for their times."»

Al-Bazzār said: nothing is narrated from Jābir except by this route.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Ḥātim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself﴾, that he said: "From shirk (polytheism)." ﴿And remembers the name of his Lord﴾: "He affirmed the oneness of God, and prayed." He said: "These are the five prayers."

Al-Bayhaqī in al-Asmā' wa-l-Ṣifāt narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself﴾: "Whoever says there is no god but God."

Al-Bazzār, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim in al-Kunā, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan narrated from Kathīr ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Amr ibn 'Awf, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet ﷺ, «that he used to command the giving of zakat al-fiṭr before performing the Eid prayer, and would recite this verse: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself and remembers the name of his Lord and prays﴾.»

In another wording he said: «The Prophet ﷺ was asked about zakat al-fiṭr, and he said: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself﴾, and said: "It is zakat al-fiṭr."» Kathīr ibn 'Abd Allāh is extremely weak. Abu Dawud said about him: "He is one of the pillars of lying." Al-Tirmidhī authenticated a hadith through his route, but he was wrongly corrected in that. However, what Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Sa'īd al-Khudrī supports it, who said: «The Messenger of God ﷺ used to say: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself and remembers the name of his Lord and prays﴾, then he would distribute the fiṭr (charity) before going out to the prayer-place on the day of Fiṭr.» There is nothing in these two hadiths indicating that this was the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzūl); rather, in them the Prophet ﷺ recited the verse. His saying "It is zakat al-fiṭr" may mean that it is among the things to which the term tazakkī (purification) applies. We have already stated that the surah is Meccan, and there was no Eid prayer or fiṭra in Mecca.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu Sa'īd al-Khudrī regarding ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself﴾, that he said: "He gave the charity of fiṭr before going out to the Eid." ﴿And remembers the name of his Lord and prays﴾: "He went out to the Eid and prayed."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī narrated from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "This verse was only revealed about giving the charity of fiṭr before the Eid prayer: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself﴾ ﴿and remembers the name of his Lord and prays﴾."

Ibn Abi Ḥātim narrated from 'Aṭā': I said to Ibn 'Abbas: "What do you think of His saying ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself﴾ as referring to fiṭr?" He said: "I have not heard of that, but [it refers] to all zakat." Then I returned to him and he said to me: "And all charities."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ṭabarānī, and al-Bayhaqī in Shu'ab al-Īmān narrated from 'Arfaja al-Thaqafī, who said: "I asked Ibn Mas'ūd to recite ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ for me. When he reached ﴿But you prefer the worldly life﴾, he stopped reading and turned to his companions and said: 'We have preferred the world over the Hereafter.' The people were silent. He said: 'We preferred the world because we saw its adornment, its women, its food, and its drink, and the Hereafter was hidden from us, so we chose this immediate thing and left the deferred one.'" And he recited "bal yu'thirūna al-ḥayāt al-dunyā" (بَلْ يُؤْثِرُونَ الحَياةَ الدُّنْيا) with a ya' (the third-person form).

Al-Bazzār, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scriptures, the scriptures of Abraham and Moses﴾: the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "All of it is in the scriptures of Abraham and Moses."

Sa'īd ibn Manṣūr, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥātim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him regarding the verse, that he said: "This surah was copied (nusikhat) from the scriptures of Abraham and Moses." In another wording: "This surah is in the scriptures of Abraham and Moses."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn 'Asākir narrated from Abu Dharr, who said: «I said: "O Messenger of God, how many books did God send down?" He said: "A hundred books and four books." » [the hadith continues].

* *

[p. 1614] Ibn al-Ḍurays, al-Naḥḥās, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The Surah al-Ghāshiyah was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated similar from Ibn al-Zubayr. It has already been mentioned the hadith of al-Nu'mān ibn Bashīr: «that the Messenger of God ﷺ used to recite ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ and al-Ghāshiyah in the Eid prayer and on Friday.»

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying ﴿Has there reached you the news of the Overwhelming (al-Ghāshiyah)?﴾: a group of exegetes said: "Has" here means "qad" (indeed, certainly). This is also the view of Qutrub. The meaning: "Indeed there has come to you, O Muhammad, the news of the Overwhelming," and the Overwhelming is the Resurrection, because it overwhelms creation with its terrors.

It has been said that retaining the interrogative meaning of "Has" here, which includes amazement at what its report contains and arousing eagerness to hear it, is more preferable.

Most exegetes have adopted that the Overwhelming here refers to the Resurrection.

Sa'īd ibn Jubayr and Muḥammad ibn Ka'b said: "The Overwhelming is the Fire, which overwhelms the faces of the disbelievers, as in His saying ﴿and the Fire will overwhelm their faces﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 50]." It has also been said that the Overwhelming means the people of the Fire, because they overwhelm it and plunge into it. The first view is more preferable.

Al-Kalbī said: the meaning is, if the news of the Overwhelming had not reached you, then it has now reached you.

﴿Faces on that Day will be humbled﴾: this sentence is resumptive (mustaʾnafah), an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What is it?" Or it is resumptive in the grammatical sense (istiʾnāf naḥwī) to explain what the event contains of [a condition], then faces on that day are described by this described attribute. "Faces" (wujūh) is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), even though it is indefinite, because it occurs in a context of detail (maqām al-tafṣīl). Something similar has been mentioned before in Surah al-Qiyāmah and Surah al-Nāzi'āt.

The tanwīn (nunation) in yawma'idhin (يَوْمَئِذٍ) is a replacement (ʿiwaḍ) for the genitive noun that is omitted: that is, "the day of the coming of the Overwhelming." Khāshi'ah means humbled, subdued. Every humbled, still thing is called khāshi'. It is said khasha'a al-ṣawt (the voice became subdued) when it became faint, and khasha'a fī ṣalātihi (he was humble in his prayer) when he abased himself and lowered his head.

The word "faces" here refers to their owners.

Muqātil said: it means the disbelievers, because they were arrogant about worshipping God.

Qatāda and Ibn Zayd said: "Humbled in the Fire." It has also been said that it refers specifically to the faces of the Jews and Christians.

The first view is more preferable.

His saying ﴿Laboring, toiling﴾: the meaning of "'āmilah" (laboring) is that they perform arduous work.

The lexicographers said: it is said of a man who persists in his journey: "He labored (ʿamila yaʿmalu ʿamalan)," and it is said of a cloud when its lightning persists: "It has labored (qad ʿamila yaʿmalu ʿamalan)."

It has been said that this work is dragging chains and shackles and wading through the Fire. *Nāṣibah* means weary (*taʿibah*). It is said *nasiba* (with a kasra) *yansabu nasaban*, meaning he became weary. The meaning is that in the Hereafter they will be weary because of what they encounter of Allah's punishment.

It has also been said that His words ﴿working, toiling﴾ refer to this world, since there is no work in the Hereafter. That is, they labour in this world in disbelief and sin, and they toil in that.

It has also been said that they labour in this world and toil in the Hereafter. The first view is preferable.

Qatadah said: ﴿Working, toiling﴾ means that they were arrogant in this world toward obedience to Allah, so Allah made them labour and toil in the Fire by dragging heavy chains, carrying shackles, and standing barefoot and naked in the open plains ﴿on a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Maʿārij: 4]. Al-Ḥasan and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: they did not labour for Allah in this world and did not toil, so Allah made them labour and toil in Jahannam.

Al-Kalbi said: they will be dragged on their faces in the Fire.

He also said: they will be burdened with climbing a mountain of iron in Jahannam, and they will toil there with the utmost toil, handling chains and shackles and wading through the Fire, as camels wade through mud.

The majority of readers (*qurrāʾ*, reciters; *qirāʾāt*, recitations, meaning the authorised variant readings of the Qur'an) read ﴿working, toiling﴾ with *rafʿ* (nominative) in both words, on the basis that they are two further predicates of the subject, or on the basis of an implied subject, and they are predicates of it. Ibn Muḥaysin, ʿĪsā, Ḥumayd, and Ibn Kathīr in one narration from him read both with *naṣb* (accusative), as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) or as a term of blame (*dhamm*).

His words ﴿they will enter a blazing Fire﴾ are another predicate of the subject. That is, they will enter a fire extremely intense in heat. It is said *ḥamiya al-nahār* and *ḥamiya al-tannūr*, meaning their heat intensified.

Al-Kisāʾi said: it is said *ishtadda ḥamy al-nahār* and *ḥamwuhu*, with the same meaning.

The majority read *taṣlā* with a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ*, in the active voice. Abu ʿAmr, Yaʿqub, and Abu Bakr read both *tuṣlā* and *tusqā* with a *ḍammah*, in the passive voice.

Abu Rajāʾ read it with a *ḍammah* on the *tāʾ*, a *fatḥah* on the *ṣād*, and a *shaddah* on the *lām*. The pronoun refers to the faces (*wujūh*) in all these recitations, and the intended meaning is their owners, as mentioned earlier. The same applies to the pronoun.

﴿They will be given drink from a boiling spring﴾. What is meant by the boiling spring (*ʿayn āniyah*) is one extremely intense in heat. *Ānī* is that which has reached its utmost heat, from *al-īnāʾ*, meaning delay. It is said *ānāhu yuʾnīhi īnāʾan*, meaning he delayed and detained him, as in His words: ﴿They will go round between it and a scalding, boiling water﴾ [al-Raḥmān: 44]. Al-Wāḥidi said: the commentators said that if a single drop of it fell on the mountains of this world, they would melt.

When He, glorified is He, mentioned their drink, He followed it with mention of their food, saying: ﴿They will have no food except from ḍarīʿ﴾. *Ḍarīʿ* is a kind of thorny plant called *shibriq* in the language of Quraysh when it is fresh; when it dries out, it becomes *ḍarīʿ*.

Mujāhid, Qatadah, and other commentators said this.

It has been said that it is a deadly poison, and that when it dries out no animal approaches it or grazes on it. It has also been said that it is something the sea casts up, called *ḍarīʿ*, which is food for livestock and not for people. When camels graze on it they do not become sated and perish from emaciation.

Al-Khalīl said: *ḍarīʿ* is a green plant with a foul smell that the sea casts up.

The majority of the lexicographers and commentators said the first view. From it is the verse of Abū Dhuʾayb:

*He grazed on the lush shibriq until it withered and became ḍarīʿ, and the tahāyis [a kind of bramble] departed from it.*

And al-Hudhalī, describing camels and their poor pasture, said:

*A pen of withered ḍarīʿ, and all of them are thin, with scraped hides, bloodied in both forelegs, and worn.*

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: *ḍarīʿ* means stones. It has also been said that it is a tree in the Fire of Jahannam.

Al-Ḥasan said: it is part of the punishment that Allah has kept hidden.

Ibn Kaysān said: it is a food at which they humble themselves, abase themselves, and beseech Allah to be delivered from it. It is named so because whoever eats it implores Allah to spare him, because of its repulsiveness and harshness.

Al-Naḥḥās said: it may be derived from *al-ḍāriʿ*, meaning the humble one. That is, from drinking it one is afflicted with humility and abasement.

Al-Ḥasan also said: it is *al-zaqqūm*. It has also been said that it is a valley in Jahannam. This has already been mentioned in Sūrat al-Ḥāqqah: ﴿So today he has no friend here, nor any food except from ghislīn﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 35–36]. *Ghislīn* is other than *ḍarīʿ*, as mentioned previously. The two verses were reconciled by saying that the Fire has levels (*darakāt*): some of its people have *ḍarīʿ* as their food, and others have *ghislīn*.

Then He, glorified is He, described *ḍarīʿ*, saying: ﴿It neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger﴾. That is, *ḍarīʿ* does not fatten the one who eats it, nor does it relieve the hunger he has.

The commentators said: when this verse was revealed, the polytheists said: our camels grow fat on *ḍarīʿ*. Then ﴿It neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger﴾ was revealed. They lied in what they said, for camels do not eat *ḍarīʿ* and do not go near it.

It has also been said that its nature was confused for them, so they assumed it was like other beneficial plants.

Then He, glorified is He, began to explain the state of the people of Paradise after finishing with the state of the people of the Fire, saying: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant﴾. That is, possessing blessing and brightness. These are the faces of the believers, whose faces became radiant because of what they witnessed of the outcome of their affair and of what Allah has prepared for them of good that exceeds description. A similar verse is His words: ﴿You will recognise in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾ [al-Muṭaffifīn: 24].

Then He said: ﴿Pleased with their striving﴾. That is, pleased with the deed they performed in this world, because they have been given reward that satisfied them and gladdened their eyes. Here "faces" refers to their owners, as mentioned earlier.

﴿In an elevated Garden﴾. That is, elevated in place, raised above other places; or elevated in rank, because in it is what souls desire and eyes delight in.

﴿In which they will hear no idle talk﴾. Al-Jumhūr read *lā tasmaʿu* with a *fatḥah* on the second-person *tāʾ* and *naṣb* on *lāghiyah*, meaning: you, O addressee, will not hear, or those faces will not hear.

Ibn Kathīr and Abu ʿAmr read it with a *ḍammah* on the *yāʾ*, in the passive voice, and *rafʿ* on *lāghiyah*.

Nāfiʿ read it with a *ḍammah* on the *tāʾ*, in the passive voice, and *rafʿ* on *lāghiyah*.

Al-Faḍl and al-Jaḥdarī read it with a *fatḥah* on the *yāʾ*, in the active voice, and *naṣb* on *lāghiyah*.

*Laghw* is futile, fallen speech. Al-Farrāʾ and al-Akhfash said: that is, they will not hear in it a word of idle talk.

It has been said that what is meant is lies, falsehood, and disbelief. Qatadah said this. Mujāhid said: that is, insult.

Al-Farrāʾ said: they will not hear in it one swearing an oath falsely.

Al-Kalbi said: they will not hear in Paradise anyone swearing an oath, whether a truthful or a sinful one.

Al-Farrāʾ also said: they will not hear in the speech of the people of Paradise any word that is idle, because they speak only with wisdom and praise of Allah, exalted is He, for what He has provided them of everlasting bliss. This is the most preferred of the views, because an indefinite noun in a negative context is a form of generality, and there is no basis for restricting this to a particular kind of idle talk except by a specifier that is suitable for restriction. *Lāghiyah* is either an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning *kalimah lāghiyah* (an idle word) or *nafs lāghiyah* (an idle soul), or a verbal noun, meaning: they will not hear in it *laghwan* (idle talk).

﴿In it is a flowing spring﴾. It has already been mentioned in Sūrat al-Insān that in it are springs, and *ʿayn* here carries the meaning of *ʿuyūn* (springs), as in His words: ﴿Every soul will know﴾ [al-Takwīr: 14]. *Jāriyah* (flowing) means that its waters flow and gush forth with kinds of delicious drinks.

Al-Kalbi said: I do not know whether it is water or something else.

﴿In it are raised couches﴾. That is, lofty, high in height; or lofty in rank.

﴿And cups placed [ready]﴾. It has already been mentioned that *akwāb* is the plural of *kūb*, which is a cup without a handle. *Mawḍūʿah* (placed) means they are placed before them, from which they drink.

﴿And cushions arranged in rows﴾. *Namāriq* are cushions.

Al-Wāḥidi said: by the agreement of all, its singular is *numruqah* with a *ḍammah* on the *nūn*. Al-Farrāʾ added, from the Arabs by hearing, *nimriqah* with a *kasrah*.

Al-Kalbi said: cushions arranged, some next to others. From this is the poet's saying:

*Indeed we pass the cup among our drinking companions, and between Abū Qābūs upon the cushions.*

And another said:

*Elders and youths, beautiful of face, upon couches arranged in rows, and cushions.*

In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* it is said: *al-numruq* and *al-nimriqah* is a small cushion, and likewise *al-nimriqah* with a *kasrah* is a dialect reported by Yaʿqūb.

﴿And carpets spread out﴾. This means rugs. Its singular is *zurbī* and *zurbiyyah*.

Abū ʿUbaydah and al-Farrāʾ said: *al-zarābī* are the cloths with a fine nap, its singular being *zarbiyyah*. *Mabthūthah* means spread out; Qatadah said this.

Ikrimah said: some of them upon others.

Al-Wāḥidi said: it could also mean that they are scattered throughout the gatherings. Al-Qutaybi said this too.

Al-Farrāʾ said: the meaning of *mabthūthah* is abundant. The apparent meaning of *al-baththu* is dispersal with abundance, as in His words: ﴿And He spread throughout them every kind of creature﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164].

﴿Will they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach, and the *fāʾ* is for coordination with an implied element, as in its parallels that have occurred more than once. The sentence is directed toward establishing the matter of resurrection and providing evidence for it, and so is what follows. *Kayfa* is in the accusative, governed by what follows it, and the clause is in the genitive position, as a substitute of inclusion (*badal ishtimāl*) for "camels." The meaning: do they deny the matter of resurrection and consider its occurrence far-fetched? Will they not look at the camels, which are the majority of their livestock and the greatest of the creatures they see, ﴿how they were created﴾ in the wondrous creation they have, with the greatness of their bodies, their great strength, and their wondrous attributes?

Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said: He specified camels because they are among the quadrupeds that kneel down so that the loads can be put on them, whereas other quadrupeds are not loaded unless they are standing. Al-Zajjāj said: He alerted them to a great creature of His creation, which He has made docile for the small child: he leads it, makes it kneel, makes it rise, and carries heavy loads on it while it is kneeling, so it rises with the weight of its load. No other load-bearing animal does this. Thus He showed them a great part of His creation, so that by this it would point to His oneness.

Al-Ḥasan was asked about this verse, and it was said to him that the elephant is more wondrous. He said: as for the elephant, the Arabs are far removed from it in time; moreover, it is a pig that is not ridden on its back, its meat is not eaten, and its milk is not milked. Camels are among the most valuable and precious property of the Arabs: they eat date pits and fodder, they yield milk, and a boy takes hold of their halter and leads them wherever he wishes, despite their great size in themselves.

Al-Mubarrad said: *al-ibil* here means great pieces of cloud. This differs from what the commentators and lexicographers have mentioned.

It is related from al-Aṣmaʿī that he said: whoever reads *khuliqat* with the light form means the camel, and whoever reads it with the doubled form means the clouds.

﴿And at the sky, how it was raised﴾. That is, raised above the earth without pillars, in a manner that understanding cannot grasp and the intellect cannot comprehend. It has been said: it was raised so that nothing can reach it.

﴿And at the mountains, how they were set firm﴾ on the earth, fixed and firmly rooted, not swaying, not leaning, and not moving.

﴿And at the earth, how it was spread out﴾. That is, it was spread flat. *Saṭḥ* is the spreading of a thing; it is said of the roof of a house when it is level: *saṭḥ*.

Al-Jumhūr read *suṭiḥat* in the passive voice, lightened. Al-Ḥasan read it with the doubled form.

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ, and Abū al-ʿĀliyah read: *khalaqtu, rafaʿtu, naṣabtu, saṭaḥtu*, in the active voice, with a *ḍammah* on the *tāʾ* in all of them.

Then He, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to remind, saying: ﴿So remind﴾. The *fāʾ* indicates the sequence of what follows relative to what precedes: that is, admonish them, O Muḥammad, and warn them.

Then He gave the reason for the command to remind, saying: ﴿You are only a reminder﴾. That is, nothing is incumbent upon you except that.

﴿You are not over them a controller﴾. *Al-muṣayṭir* and *al-musayṭir*, with *sīn* and *ṣād*, means one empowered over a thing to oversee it and attend to its affairs, as stated in *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*. That is: you are not over them a controller, to the point of compelling them to faith. This verse has been abrogated by the verse of the sword.

Al-Jumhūr read *bi-muṣayṭir* with a *ṣād*. Hishām and Qunbul in one narration read it with a *sīn*.

Khalaf read it with the *ṣād* pronounced as a *zāy* (*ishmām*).

Hārūn al-Aʿwar read it with a *fatḥah* on the *ṭāʾ* as a passive participle.

﴿Except for whoever turns away and disbelieves﴾. This is an exceptive clause of disconnection (*istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ*). That is: but whoever turns away from admonition and reminder.

﴿So Allah will punish him with the greatest punishment﴾, which is the everlasting punishment of Hell. It has also been said that this is a continuous exception (istithna' muttasil) from His words ﴿so remind﴾, meaning: remind everyone except the one whose hope of his faith you have lost and who turns away, and so deserves the greatest punishment. The first view is preferable.

He said "the greatest" because they were punished in this world by hunger, drought, killing and captivity.

Ibn Mas'ud recited ﴿Indeed, it is He who will punish him﴾ (fa-innahu yu'adhdhibuhu Allah). Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah recited "Alā man tawallā" (Surely whoever turns away), taking "alā" as the particle of alerting and opening (al-tanbih wa al-istiftah).

﴿Indeed, to Us is their return﴾, i.e., their coming back after death. It is said: āba yaūbu, meaning he returned. From this is the saying of 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras:

*Every absent one returns, but the absence of death does not return.*

The majority (al-Jumhur) read *iyābahum* with a light pronunciation (takhfif). Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read it with a doubled letter (tashdid).

Abu Hatim said: the doubling is not permissible; if it were, its equivalent would be permissible in *al-siyām* and *al-qiyām*. It has also been said that both are two dialects with the same meaning.

al-Wahidi said: as for *iyābahum* with a doubled yā', it is anomalous (shādh), and no one permitted it except al-Zajjaj.

﴿Then indeed upon Us is their reckoning﴾, meaning their recompense after their return to Allah through resurrection. *Thumma* (then) here indicates a delay in rank, because the station of reckoning is far greater in severity than the station of return.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "al-Ghashiyah" is among the names of the Resurrection.

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him regarding ﴿Has there come to you the news of the Overwhelming?﴾, that it is the Hour. ﴿Faces that Day will be humbled, labouring and weary﴾: he said, they will labour and toil in the Fire. ﴿Given to drink from a boiling spring﴾: he said, it is the one whose heat has reached its extreme. ﴿They will have no food except from *dari'*﴾: he said, it is *al-shibriq*.

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him: ﴿Faces that Day will be humbled, labouring and weary﴾, he said: this means the Jews and Christians, who humble themselves, but their deeds will not benefit them. ﴿Given to drink from a boiling spring﴾: he said, its boiling has reached its end.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him regarding His words ﴿They will burn in a fierce fire﴾: he said, hot. ﴿Given to drink from a boiling spring﴾: he said, its heat has reached its limit. ﴿They will have no food except from *dari'*﴾: he means, from a tree of fire.

'Abd ibn Humayd also narrated from him: ﴿except from *dari'*﴾, he said: dried *shibriq*.

Ibn Jarir also narrated from him: ﴿Therein they will hear no idle talk﴾, meaning they will hear neither harm nor falsehood. Regarding His words ﴿Therein are raised couches﴾, he said: some above others. ﴿And cushions set out﴾, he said: gatherings.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him: ﴿And cushions set out﴾, he said: the armrests (al-marafiq).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him regarding ﴿You are not over them a controller﴾: he said, a tyrant. ﴿Except one who turns away and disbelieves﴾: he said, his reckoning is upon Allah.

Abu Dawud, in his book *al-Nasikh*, narrated from him regarding ﴿You are not over them a controller﴾ that it was then abrogated (nasakha) by His words: ﴿So kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5].

Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him regarding ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return﴾: he said, their place of return.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 87, verses 1–19 (part 1 of 4):

It is Meccan according to the majority of scholars.

Al-Dahhak said: it is Medinan.

Ibn al-Duraysi, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "The surah ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn al-Zubayr and ʿAʾishah something similar.

Al-Bukhari and others transmitted from al-Baraʾ ibn ʿAzib that he said: "The first of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ to come to us was Musʿab ibn ʿUmayr and Ibn Umm Maktum. They began teaching us the Qur'an. Then ʿAmmar, Bilal and Saʿd came. Then ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab came with twenty men. Then the Prophet ﷺ came. I have never seen the people of Medina rejoice at anything as they rejoiced at him, until I saw the young women and children saying, 'This is the Messenger of God ﷺ, who has come.' He had not arrived until I had recited ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ and a surah like it."

Ahmad, al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from ʿAli that he said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ loved this surah: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾."

Ahmad, Muslim and the authors of the Sunan transmitted from al-Nuʿman ibn Bashir that "the Messenger of God ﷺ used to recite in the two ʿIds and on Friday ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ and ﴿Has there come to you the report of the Overwhelming?﴾. If the ʿId fell on a Friday, he recited both of them together." In another wording: "Sometimes both came together on one day, and he recited them both." There are other hadiths on this topic.

Muslim and others transmitted from Jabir ibn Samurah that "the Prophet ﷺ used to recite ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ in the noon prayer."

Abu Dawud, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Majah, al-Daraqutni, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that he said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ used to pray the witr with ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾, ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾, and ﴿Say: He is God, One﴾."

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim (who authenticated it) and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from ʿAʾishah that she said: "The Prophet ﷺ used to recite in the witr, in the first rakʿah, ﴿Glorify﴾, in the second ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾, and in the third ﴿Say: He is God, One﴾ and the two protective surahs." In the two Sahihs it is reported that the Messenger of God ﷺ said to Muʿadh: "Why did you not pray with ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾, ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾, and ﴿By the night when it covers﴾?" [i.e., Surah al-Layl].

[p-1611]
In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

His words: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾, meaning: declare Him free of everything that is not fitting for Him.

Al-Suddi said: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ means: magnify Him. It has been said that the word "name" (ism) here is superfluous (muqhamah), for the purpose of glorification, as in the verse of Labid:

*Until the year is complete, then "the name of peace be upon you both,"*
*and whoever weeps for a full year has excused himself.*

The meaning is: glorify your Lord, the Most High.

Ibn Jarir said: the meaning is, "Declare the name of your Lord free of being named by anyone other than Him." Thus, on this view, it is not superfluous.

It has also been said that the meaning is: declare the naming of your Lord and your mention of Him free of [being mentioned] except with humility and reverence, and with respect for His remembrance.

Al-Hasan said: the meaning of ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ is: pray to Him.

It has been said the meaning is: pray with the names of God, not as the polytheists pray, with whistling and clapping.

It has also been said the meaning is: raise your voice in the remembrance of your Lord. From this is the verse of Jarir:

*May God disfigure the faces of Taghlib, whenever*
*the pilgrims glorify and magnify with great magnification.*

"The Most High" (al-aʿla) is an attribute of the Lord, and it has been said it is an attribute of "name." The first view is preferable.

His words: ﴿Who created and proportioned﴾ are another attribute of the Lord.

Al-Zajjaj said: He created man upright, and the meaning of "proportioned" (sawwa) is that He made his stature balanced.

Al-Dahhak said: He created him and made his creation proportionate. It has been said He created bodies and made the faculties proportionate. It has been said He created man and prepared him for moral responsibility (taklif).

﴿And who determined and guided﴾ is another attribute of the Lord, or it is coordinated (maʿtuf) with the relative clause before it.

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, al-Kisaʾi and al-Sulami read "qadara" (determined) with light stress (mukhaffafan), while the rest read it with the doubled letter (al-tashdid). Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: He determined the creation of the male and female of the animals, and He guided the male to the female, [showing him] how to approach her.

Mujahid said: He guided man to the path of good and evil, and to happiness and misery.

It is also reported from him that he said regarding the meaning of the verse: He determined happiness and misery, and He guided to right guidance and to error, and He guided the livestock to their pasturage.

It has been said He determined their provisions and sustenance, and guided them to their livelihoods if they were human, and to their pasture if they were wild.

ʿAtaʾ said: For every creature was provided what sustains it, and He guided it to it.

It has been said He created the benefits in things, and guided man to the method of extracting them from them.

Al-Suddi said: He determined the duration of the fetus in the womb as nine months, or less or more, then He guided it to come out of the womb.

Al-Farraʾ said: That is, He determined and guided, and He led astray, and one of the two was sufficient. There are views on the interpretation of the verse other than those we have mentioned.

The preferable view is not to specify one individual or several of what the words "determined" and "guided" might apply to, unless there is evidence indicating it. In the absence of evidence, the verse is taken to refer to whatever the meaning of the two verbs covers, either by substitution (ʿala al-badal) or by comprehensiveness (ʿala al-shumul). The meaning is: He determined the kinds of things, their species, their attributes, their actions, their words, and their terms, and He guided each one of them to what proceeds from it and what befits it, facilitated for it what it was created for, and inspired it toward the affairs of its religion and its worldly life.

﴿And who brought forth the pasture﴾ is another attribute of the Lord: that is, He caused the herbage and the green vegetation that livestock graze to grow.

﴿Then made it dry stubble, dark⟩ — that is, after it had been green, He made it stubble, meaning dried, brittle debris like the scum that lies atop a flood; ﴿dark﴾ means black after its greenness. This is because when herbage dries it turns black.

Qatadah said: "Ghuthaʾ" is dry matter. It is said of the green herb and grass when it is crushed and dried: "ghuthaʾ" and "hashim" (dry brittle stalks).

Imru al-Qays said:

*As if the peaks of the head of al-Mujaymir at morning*
*were, from the flood and the scum, a spindle whorl.*

The accusative of "ghuthaʾ" is either as the second object, or as a circumstantial accusative (hal). "Ahwa" is an attribute of it.

Al-Kisaʾi said: It is a circumstantial accusative from "the pasture": that is, He brought it forth dark from the intensity of greenness and moisture, then made it stubble after that. "Ahwa" is derived from "al-hawwa," which is blackness tending toward green.

Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: "al-hawwah" is the darkness of the lip, and from this is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

*A honey-lipped one, on whose lips is the darkness of the lips' dark sweetness,*
*and on her gums and her fangs is a sweet coolness.*

﴿We shall make you recite, so you will not forget﴾: that is, We shall make you a reciter by inspiring you to recite, so you will not forget what you recite. The sentence is resumed (mustaʾnafah), explaining his special guidance ﷺ after the explanation of general guidance; it is his guidance ﷺ for memorizing the Qur'an.

Mujahid and al-Kalbi said: "When Gabriel came to the Prophet ﷺ with revelation, Gabriel would not finish the last part of the verse before the Prophet ﷺ began speaking the first part of it, for fear that he would forget it. So the verse ﴿We shall make you recite, so you will not forget﴾ was revealed."

His words: ﴿except what God wills﴾ are an exception of the "emptied" type (istithnaʾ mufarragh, i.e., an exception where the excluded element is left unspecified) from the most general of the objects: that is, you will not forget any of the things you recite, except what God wills that you forget.

Al-Farraʾ said: He, glorified be He, did not will that Muhammad ﷺ forget anything, like His saying: ﴿Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾ [Hud: 107]. It has also been said: except what God wills that you forget and then remember afterwards. Thus he has forgotten, but he remembers, and he does not forget anything with complete forgetfulness.

It has been said the meaning is abrogation (naskh): that is, except what God wills to abrogate its recitation.

It has been said the meaning of "so you will not forget" is: so do not abandon acting upon it, except what God wills that you abandon because of its abrogation and the lifting of its ruling.

It has been said the meaning is: except what God wills to delay its sending down.

It has been said that "lā" in His saying ﴿so you will not forget﴾ is a prohibition (nahy). The alif is added for the sake of the rhyme (fasila), as in His saying: ﴿So they led us astray from the way﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67]. That is, do not neglect its recitation, and remember it.

﴿Indeed He knows the open and what is hidden﴾: the sentence is a justification (taʿlil) for what precedes it, that is: He knows what appears and what is concealed, and what is proclaimed and what is kept secret. Its apparent meaning is generality, so it includes what has been said: the "open" is what the Messenger of God ﷺ memorized of the Qur'an, and "what is hidden" is what was abrogated from his breast. It also includes what has been said: the "open" is the public declaration of charity, and "what is hidden" is concealing it. It also includes what has been said: the "open" is his ﷺ reciting the Qur'an aloud along with Gabriel's recitation, for fear that it might slip from him, and "what is hidden" is what is in his soul that calls him to recite aloud.

﴿And We shall ease you toward ease﴾ is coordinated with ﴿We shall make you recite﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (iʿtiraḍ).

Muqatil said: that is, We shall make the work of Paradise easy for you. It has been said: We shall grant you success in the way that is easiest and simplest. It has been said: [We shall grant you success for] the easy Law, which is the simple, straight religion (al-hanifiyyah al-samhah). It has been said: We shall make the revelation easy for you, until you memorize it and act upon it. The preferable view is to take the verse in its generality: that is, We shall grant you success in the easiest path, in religion and in worldly life, in every matter of the two that comes before you.
